```{r setup}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)

# Render from the project root so these relative paths work
clean_log <- read_csv("outputs/tables/data_cleaning_log.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

## S1. Data preparation

The workbook gives, for each station and year, nematode composition in two sediment layers, along with summary indices and environmental measurements. The 2010 values are percentages and the 2011 values are counts of roughly 100 animals per sample, so we compare composition and not abundance, and every sample was converted to percent of its own total. The two layers at a station come from the same spot, so they were averaged and each station in each year was treated as one observation. Genus lists differ between years partly because of spelling and identification detail, so comparisons between years use families.

Table S1 reproduces the cleaning log written by the data preparation script. A few entries affect how results should be read. The 2010 maturity index row in the workbook repeats one value across many samples and looks like a copy error, so we recalculated the index from the cleaned data. The maturity index and the index of trophic diversity are calculated from the same genus composition we analyze, so they add no independent information and we did not model them. The hydrocarbon and metal measurements look to be on very different scales in the two years, which is why we did not use environmental variables in the main models.

```{r cleaning-log}
clean_log |>
  rename(Step = step, Issue = issue, `What we did` = action) |>
  kable(caption = "Table S1. Cleaning decisions and flags recorded during data preparation.")
```

## S2. Open questions about the dataset

Some questions remain that bear on how far the results can be pushed. We do not know whether sampling, subsampling, and identification methods were the same in both years, which matters because every station, including the controls, shifted between 2010 and 2011. We do not know what units the hydrocarbon and metal measurements use in each year. We also do not know whether later surveys exist that are comparable to these, which would allow recovery to be followed over a longer period.
